text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This looks like a public goods game with negative externalities affecting private holdings. I'm working out the payoff math: tokens kept private give me 1 point each but reduce others by 0.75 each, while tokens contributed to the group give me 0.75 with no negative effect on others, so I'm calculating my total points based on how much I keep versus contribute and how much others keep privately.

Doing the math, keeping tokens private is individually dominant each round since 1 > 0.75, but socially destructive—full defection yields -25 points per person versus +15 each if everyone cooperates fully. Since this is a repeated 10-round game, I'm leaning toward opening with full cooperation (contributing everything to the group) to signal good faith, then adjusting my strategy based on how the group responds.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the public goods game payoffs: each token kept privately yields 1 point to self but costs others 0.75 each, while contributing to the group account yields 0.75 to everyone. I'm setting up the formula for my own payoff based on how much I keep versus contribute, aiming to compare individual versus group-optimal strategies.

Keeping everything turns out to be individually dominant since each kept token nets +0.25 after accounting for the loss from others' contributions, but this leads to a much worse outcome for everyone (20 points each) compared to full cooperation (60 points each). I'm now considering whether to act cooperatively anyway, especially if the game might be repeated.

Working it out, cooperating fully nets me 15 if everyone else defects, versus 20 from keeping everything—only a 5 point cost. But if everyone cooperates, I'd earn 60 compared to 20 under mutual defection, so it's worth opening with full cooperation. I'll put in 20.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the public goods game payoffs: keeping a token privately nets +1 for me but costs each of the other three members 0.75, while putting a token in the group account gives everyone, including me, 0.75. Calculating the social optimum, if all 80 tokens go into the group account, each member's total payoff comes from 0.75 times that full group total.

Working through the numbers confirms full cooperation yields 15 each plus the 45 base, far better than everyone defecting which nets -25. So the socially optimal move is clear even though individually keeping tokens dominates. Given this is a repeated game over 10 rounds, I'll start cooperatively by contributing my full 20 tokens to the group account, likely adjusting later based on how others respond.

reply.thinking:

I'm checking what happens if everyone fully cooperates, calculating that each member would net 15 points from the group share.

Working through the math either way, keeping tokens individually dominates since it yields more to self while imposing costs on others — a classic social dilemma where group contribution is collectively optimal but individually tempting to defect from. Despite the incentive to free-ride, contributing to the group account seems like the cooperative, mutually beneficial choice worth leaning toward.

calls.text: Round 2 of 10. Last round you put 20 tokens in the group account, it received 80 in total, and you got 60 points.

reply.thinking:
Everyone contributed all 20, confirming full cooperation, and I netted 60 points as expected. I'm weighing whether defecting next round—keeping my 20 private while others likely cooperate again—could net me 65 instead, a tempting 5-point gain, but that risks breaking the cooperative dynamic.

Since sustained cooperation benefits the group most, I'll stick with a tit-for-tat approach and keep contributing my full 20.
